headings.title: Introduction to Corticosteroids and Mechanism of Action
headings.content: Corticosteroids, commonly referred to as steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, are synthetic analogs of hormones produced naturally by the adrenal cortex, specifically glucocorticoids like cortisol. As nursing students in Nigeria preparing for professional examinations, it is essential to understand that these powerful medications play a critical role in modulating immune and inflammatory responses within the human body. The primary mechanism of action centers on their interaction with intracellular glucocorticoid receptors. Once a corticosteroid binds to its specific cytosolic receptor, the drug-receptor complex translocates into the cell nucleus. Here, it interacts directly with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) to either upregulate anti-inflammatory gene expression or, more commonly, downregulate pro-inflammatory gene transcription. A key enzymatic target in this pathway is phospholipase A2, which is inhibited indirectly through the induction of a protein called lipocortin-1 (annexin A1). By inhibiting phospholipase A2, corticosteroids block the release of arachidonic acid from cell membranes, effectively halting the entire arachidonic acid cascade. This suppression prevents the downstream formation of both prostaglandins, which mediate pain and vasodilation, and leukotrienes, which are potent mediators of bronchoconstriction and inflammation. Furthermore, corticosteroids suppress the proliferation, differentiation, and overall function of key immune cells, including T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes, monocytes, and eosinophils. They also reduce capillary permeability, thereby minimizing tissue edema and exudation during acute inflammatory episodes. Understanding this fundamental cellular mechanism provides the pharmacological basis for why corticosteroids are exceptionally potent agents for managing acute hypersensitivity reactions, severe autoimmune flare-ups, and chronic inflammatory conditions seen frequently in clinical practice across Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: Classification and Potency of Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs
headings.content: Steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are categorized into different classes based on their relative anti-inflammatory potency, mineralocorticoid activity, and duration of action. For nursing practice, recognizing these differences ensures that clinicians administer the correct drug profile for specific clinical scenarios. Classification is broadly divided into short-acting, intermediate-acting, and long-acting agents. Short-acting corticosteroids, such as hydrocortisone and cortisone, possess a biological half-life of 8 to 12 hours and retain significant mineralocorticoid activity, meaning they affect sodium and water balance strongly. Intermediate-acting agents, including prednisolone, prednisone, methylprednisolone, and triamcinolone, have a half-life ranging from 12 to 36 hours. They exhibit a more favorable balance by offering higher anti-inflammatory potency with markedly reduced mineralocorticoid effects compared to hydrocortisone. Long-acting corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone and betamethasone, have a biological half-life extending beyond 36 to 54 hours. These agents possess immense anti-inflammatory potency—dexamethasone is roughly 25 to 30 times more potent than hydrocortisone—and virtually negligible mineralocorticoid activity. This high potency makes long-acting agents ideal for conditions requiring intense anti-inflammatory action without fluid retention, such as cerebral edema or severe COVID-19-related respiratory distress. Potency ratings are calculated relative to hydrocortisone, which serves as the baseline standard. Nurses must be vigilant when converting between different steroid formulations, as incorrect dosing due to potency miscalculation can lead to therapeutic failure or severe toxicity. Familiarity with these pharmacokinetic groupings helps anticipate the frequency of administration and potential adverse events related to electrolyte balance during patient care.

headings.title: Pharmacokinetics and Administration Routes
headings.content: The pharmacokinetics of steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs dictate how they are absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted in the body, directly influencing the choice of administration route. Corticosteroids are lipophilic molecules, which allows them to be readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract when administered orally. Oral administration, such as tablets of prednisolone, is preferred for chronic maintenance therapy due to ease of use and patient compliance. However, parenteral routes—including intravenous (IV) and intramuscular (IM) injections—are vital in emergency situations, severe acute exacerbations, or when a patient is unable to take oral medications. Intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone provides rapid systemic bioavailability, making it indispensable in life-threatening scenarios such as status asthmaticus, anaphylaxis, or acute adrenal crisis. Topical preparations, including creams, ointments, and eye drops, offer localized delivery for dermatologic conditions or ocular inflammation, minimizing systemic absorption and subsequent side effects. Inhaled corticosteroids, such as budesonide or fluticasone, are foundational in the management of chronic asthma, delivering the drug directly to the respiratory mucosa with minimal systemic spillover. Intra-articular injections, such as triamcinolone acetonide, provide high local concentrations of the drug directly into inflamed joint spaces, offering targeted relief for osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis flare-ups. Once absorbed, corticosteroids bind extensively to plasma proteins, primarily corticosteroid-binding globulin (transcortin) and albumin. They are metabolized predominantly by the liver into inactive water-soluble metabolites and are subsequently excreted via the renal system. Nursing students must understand these routes to ensure accurate medication delivery, proper patient positioning, and appropriate observation for both local and systemic adverse effects.

headings.title: Therapeutic Indications in Musculoskeletal and Systemic Disorders
headings.content: Corticosteroids possess a vast array of therapeutic indications in both musculoskeletal and systemic disorders due to their potent immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory properties. In musculoskeletal practice, they are frequently utilized to manage inflammatory joint diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and acute gouty arthritis. Intra-articular injections provide substantial pain relief and reduce synovial inflammation in localized joint flare-ups, while systemic oral courses manage widespread joint involvement. In systemic disorders, corticosteroids are cornerstones in treating autoimmune conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), where they control life-threatening nephritis, vasculitis, and serositis. They are similarly indispensable in managing inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis), severe dermatologic disorders (such as pemphigus vulgaris), and hematological malignancies or immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). In respiratory medicine, systemic or inhaled corticosteroids are vital for controlling moderate-to-severe asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations, and interstitial lung diseases by reducing airway mucosal edema and inflammatory cell infiltration. Furthermore, they are life-saving in acute allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, and primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, where physiological replacement doses are required to sustain life. In neurology, high-dose dexamethasone is prescribed to reduce vasogenic cerebral edema associated with brain tumors or bacterial meningitis. Nursing students must appreciate this diverse clinical utility because nurses are responsible for evaluating the therapeutic effectiveness of the drug against the specific pathology for which it was prescribed, ensuring patients experience optimal clinical outcomes while minimizing unnecessary exposure.

headings.title: Acute and Chronic Adverse Effects of Corticosteroid Therapy
headings.content: While corticosteroids are exceptionally effective therapeutic agents, their prolonged or high-dose use is associated with a wide spectrum of acute and chronic adverse effects. These side effects mimic the clinical features of Cushing's syndrome. Acute administration can cause neuropsychiatric disturbances, including mood swings, euphoria, insomnia, and frank psychosis, as well as acute hyperglycemia due to stimulated hepatic gluconeogenesis and peripheral insulin resistance. Gastrointestinal complications such as peptic ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding are frequent, particularly when steroids are co-administered with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Chronic corticosteroid therapy leads to profound structural and metabolic changes. Patients often develop redistribution of body fat, resulting in truncal obesity, a 'moon face,' and a 'buffalo hump.' Protein catabolism causes muscle wasting, proximal limb weakness, skin thinning, easy bruising, and purple striae. Bone metabolism is severely compromised through decreased calcium absorption in the gut, increased renal calcium excretion, and suppression of osteoblast activity, culminating in osteoporosis, pathological fractures, and avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Ophthalmic complications include posterior subcapsular cataracts and elevated intraocular pressure leading to glaucoma. Additionally, because of their potent immunosuppressive actions, corticosteroids mask the classical signs of infection, leaving patients highly vulnerable to opportunistic bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens. Fluid and electrolyte disturbances, such as sodium and water retention accompanied by potassium wasting, can induce hypertension and peripheral edema. Nursing students must maintain constant vigilance to identify these adverse effects early during routine clinical assessments.

headings.title: Contraindications, Precautions, and Drug Interactions
headings.content: The administration of steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs requires careful evaluation of patient contraindications, precautions, and potential drug-drug interactions to ensure patient safety. Absolute contraindications for systemic corticosteroid therapy are relatively few in emergency settings, but they are crucial in chronic use. They include active, untreated systemic fungal infections, known hypersensitivity to the specific drug formulation, and the administration of live or live-attenuated vaccines while on immunosuppressive doses. Precautions must be exercised in patients with underlying conditions such as diabetes mellitus (due to the risk of severe hyperglycemia), active peptic ulcer disease, hypertension, congestive heart failure, renal impairment, osteoporosis, and a history of psychiatric disturbances like severe depression or psychosis. Drug interactions can significantly alter therapeutic efficacy or escalate toxicity risks. Co-administration of corticosteroids with potassium-depleting agents, such as loop or thiazide diuretics, dramatically increases the risk of severe hypokalemia and subsequent cardiac arrhythmias. When combined with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, the risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and hemorrhage multiplies exponentially. Furthermore, hepatic enzyme inducers, such as phenobarbital, phenytoin, and rifampicin, enhance the metabolic clearance of corticosteroids, potentially reducing their anti-inflammatory efficacy and leading to disease flare-ups. Conversely, inhibitors of the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, such as ketoconazole, can decrease corticosteroid metabolism, leading to elevated plasma drug levels and increased toxicity. Nursing students must thoroughly review patient medication histories and medical diagnoses before administering these drugs to prevent dangerous adverse interactions.

headings.title: Patient Assessment and Monitoring Guidelines
headings.content: Comprehensive patient assessment and meticulous monitoring guidelines are paramount for safe nursing care during corticosteroid therapy. Baseline assessments must include a thorough medical history, physical examination, vital signs (especially blood pressure), body weight, and baseline laboratory investigations. Essential baseline labs include fasting blood glucose or HbA1c to screen for glycemic control, serum electrolytes (particularly potassium and sodium), renal function tests, liver function tests, and baseline bone density scans (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) for patients initiating long-term therapy. Throughout the course of treatment, ongoing monitoring must be systematic. Nurses should routinely check blood pressure for signs of hypertension, monitor daily weights and assess for peripheral edema to detect fluid retention, and perform regular blood glucose monitoring, especially in diabetic patients who may require adjustments to their insulin or oral hypoglycemic regimens. Periodic monitoring of serum electrolytes is necessary to detect hypokalemia. Nurses must also assess mental status for mood changes, agitation, or depressive symptoms. For pediatric patients, regular monitoring of growth and developmental milestones is critical because chronic corticosteroids suppress linear bone growth. In patients receiving long-term therapy, regular eye examinations by an optometrist or ophthalmologist are mandatory to screen for early signs of cataracts and glaucoma. Documenting and reporting these assessment findings promptly allows the interprofessional healthcare team to adjust dosages or initiate prophylactic medications, such as calcium and vitamin D supplements or proton pump inhibitors, thereby mitigating predictable complications.

headings.title: HPA Axis Suppression and Safe Tapering Protocols
headings.content: One of the most critical physiological phenomena associated with corticosteroid therapy is Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis suppression. Normally, the hypothalamus secretes corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which in turn signals the adrenal cortex to synthesize and secrete cortisol. When exogenous corticosteroids are administered over a prolonged period, typically exceeding two to three weeks, the high circulating levels of synthetic steroids exert negative feedback inhibition on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. Consequently, the endogenous production of CRH and ACTH drops significantly, and the adrenal cortex undergoes functional atrophy due to a lack of stimulation. If exogenous corticosteroids are abruptly discontinued, the atrophied adrenal glands cannot immediately resume endogenous cortisol production. This precipitates a life-threatening crisis known as acute adrenal insufficiency or an Addisonian crisis, characterized by profound hypotension, circulatory collapse, hypoglycemia, severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and confusion. To prevent this dangerous complication, safe tapering protocols must be strictly implemented whenever systemic corticosteroids are discontinued after prolonged use. Tapering involves gradually reducing the daily dose over weeks or months, allowing adequate time for the HPA axis and the adrenal cortex to recover their normal structure and function. Nurses must educate patients never to stop taking corticosteroids abruptly on their own and must closely monitor patients during the taper for signs of steroid withdrawal syndrome, which includes fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia, and orthostatic hypotension.

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities and Patient Education
headings.content: Nursing responsibilities regarding steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs extend far beyond administration; they encompass comprehensive patient education to ensure safe, effective therapy and prevent complications. Nurses must teach patients and their families the importance of taking oral corticosteroids exactly as prescribed, typically with food or milk to minimize gastric irritation and ulcer formation. Patients should be instructed to take single daily doses in the morning, usually around 8:00 AM, which mimics the body's natural circadian rhythm of cortisol secretion and helps reduce HPA axis suppression. Nurses must emphasize that patients should never alter their dose or abruptly stop taking the medication without explicit medical direction, reinforcing the necessity of safe tapering protocols. Patient education must also focus on infection prevention strategies. Because steroids mask signs of infection, patients must report any subtle signs of illness—such as a mild fever, sore throat, or unusual fatigue—immediately. They should avoid contact with individuals who have known infections and should be advised against receiving live-access vaccines. Dietary modifications should be discussed, recommending a diet high in calcium, vitamin D, and protein to counteract muscle wasting and bone demineralization, along with low sodium and potassium-rich foods to manage fluid retention. Patients should be encouraged to carry emergency identification, such as a medical alert card, indicating they are on chronic corticosteroid therapy. Finally, nurses must empower patients to monitor and report symptoms like rapid weight gain, visual disturbances, persistent indigestion, or mood alterations, fostering a collaborative approach to safe pharmacotherapy.
